assessment_summary:
At line 0197, in the proof of Theorem 2.1, the author concludes that the code C is self-dual solely because an arbitrary element v+2v' of C is orthogonal to an arbitrary element 2w of 2Tor_1(C). This only establishes that C is orthogonal to its subcode 2Tor_1(C), not that C is orthogonal to itself. To prove C is self-dual, one must show that any two elements of C are orthogonal (e.g., examining the inner product of v_1+2v_1' and v_2+2v_2'), which would leave an unverified term [v_1, v_2]_4 that is not necessarily zero. 

This logical leap is invalid, and the theorem itself is false. A simple counterexample is the Z_4 code C = \langle 11 \rangle of length 2. It has Tor_0(C) = Tor_1(C) = \{00, 11\}. Since the dual of \{00, 11\} over F_2 is \{00, 11\}, we have Tor_0(C) = Tor_1(C)^\perp. However, C is not self-dual over Z_4 because 11 \cdot 11 = 2 \neq 0 \pmod 4. Thus, 0197 is the first flawed step.
counterexample: C = \langle 11 \rangle over \ZZ_4, which has length 2 and size 4. Tor_0(C) = Tor_1(C) = \{00, 11\}. This satisfies Tor_0(C) = Tor_1(C)^\perp, but C is not self-dual since [11, 11]_4 = 2 \neq 0.
